title: Trump SoHo Buyers Sue Over Allegedly Inflated Condominium Sales Figures
description_medium: In 2010, buyers of units at Trump SoHo sued Donald Trump and other project promoters, alleging they overstated sales to make the hotel-condominium appear more successful. A filing cited by the buyers showed 62 of roughly 400 units sold, just over 15 percent, while promotional statements had suggested more than 60 percent. The claims were allegations in a civil suit, not a court finding of fraud.
description_long: Trump SoHo, a hotel-condominium development in lower Manhattan, opened during the 2008 financial crisis. In August 2010, 15 buyers sued Donald Trump, his children, and other promoters, alleging that sales claims misrepresented the project’s financial health and pressured purchasers to close. The buyers said they had been told that at least 60 percent of the roughly 400 units were sold. A condominium filing with New York State reportedly listed only 62 sales, slightly more than 15 percent. The plaintiffs argued that the gap mattered because potential buyers relied on sales figures when deciding whether to complete purchases. Trump and the other defendants denied the accusations. In 2011, the project’s sponsors settled with ten buyers, who received 90 percent of their deposits back. The settlement resolved those buyers’ claims without establishing the allegations as a court finding. A separate criminal investigation into promotional statements made by Trump’s children later ended without charges.

corrected_wording.label: Claim limitation
corrected_wording.text: Treat the inflated-sales statements as allegations by buyers. The linked source supplied for this entry does not substantiate the separate claim that a donation caused prosecutors to close an investigation.

source_access_notes: Search found same-event Reuters coverage of the lawsuit and contemporaneous reporting on the settlement; separate reporting describes the later criminal investigation.
rationale: Builds the narrative around the civil buyers’ suit and 2011 settlement, attributes the sales disparity to plaintiffs, and avoids suggesting allegations were adjudicated as fraud.

title: Trump Amplifies QAnon Slogans and Attacks on Truth Social
description_medium: In August 2024, Donald Trump reposted a stream of Truth Social messages that included QAnon slogans, calls to jail political opponents, and a sexist insinuation about Kamala Harris. The posts came as Trump’s advisers urged him to focus on policy rather than personal attacks. They showed him continuing to amplify conspiratorial language during the presidential campaign.
description_long: Over two days in late August 2024, Donald Trump reposted numerous messages on Truth Social that included QAnon phrases, calls to jail critics and political opponents, and an insinuation that Vice President Kamala Harris had advanced her career through sexual relationships. The burst of posts came as Trump’s advisers were urging him to emphasize policy on the economy and border rather than personal attacks. The messages renewed scrutiny of his willingness to amplify conspiracy-oriented accounts and retaliatory rhetoric in the middle of a presidential campaign. They also attracted attention because QAnon language had repeatedly appeared in material Trump shared on social media. This episode concerns a particular late-August posting spree; it should not be described as proof that each post was racist or antisemitic.

corrected_wording.label: Title and claim correction
corrected_wording.text: The same-event reporting supports QAnon phrases, calls to jail opponents, and a sexist insinuation; it does not substantiate the supplied claim about racist and antisemitic memes.

source_access_notes: Search found Axios’s event-specific August 29 report on the posting spree; the supplied NBC link concerns an unrelated Instagram image.
blockers: Need the specific Truth Social posts or event-matched reporting to identify the images, dates, source accounts, and response.
rationale: Retains the broad event claim with attribution and avoids inventing examples or treating an unsupported count and characterization as verified.

title: Biden Says He Is Not Confident Trump Would Accept a 2024 Election Loss
description_medium: In an August 2024 interview, President Joe Biden said he was “not confident at all” that Donald Trump would accept the results if he lost the November election. Biden pointed to Trump’s conduct after the 2020 election and his repeated claims that a loss would reflect fraud. Trump had said during the June debate that he would accept the result if the election were “fair and legal and good.”
description_long: President Joe Biden raised doubts about whether the 2024 election would end in a peaceful transfer of power in an interview broadcast in August. Asked whether he was confident the transition would be peaceful if Donald Trump lost, Biden answered, “If Trump loses, I’m not confident at all.” He cited Trump’s refusal to accept the 2020 result and his statements about what might happen if he lost again. The comments were Biden’s assessment of the risk, not evidence that a transfer would fail. During the June 2024 debate, Trump said he would accept the election result if it was “fair and legal and good,” while also repeating claims that the 2020 election had been stolen. The exchange returned attention to the peaceful transfer of power, a basic feature of democratic elections, during a campaign in which Trump continued to challenge the prior result. The linked NBC report covers Biden’s concern, not a documented blanket refusal by Trump to commit to a peaceful transfer.

corrected_wording.label: Title correction
corrected_wording.text: “Biden Says He Is Not Confident Trump Would Accept a 2024 Election Loss” reflects the linked report; the supplied title’s claim that Trump refused to commit is broader than the cited event.

source_access_notes: Search located the same CBS interview and contemporaneous report. Updated the entry to describe Biden’s stated concern rather than attribute an unsupported explicit refusal to Trump.
rationale: Corrects the event framing to the actual interview and preserves Trump’s conditional June debate response alongside Biden’s concern.

title: H-1B Visa Dispute Exposes Rift Between Trump Allies
description_medium: In December 2024, a public dispute over H-1B work visas exposed tension between technology executives supporting the program and immigration hard-liners in Donald Trump’s political coalition. Elon Musk defended the visas as important to recruiting skilled workers. President-elect Trump then said he supported the program, siding with Musk in the debate. The episode highlighted competing views inside the coalition about skilled immigration.
description_long: A dispute over H-1B visas erupted among Trump supporters in late December 2024. Elon Musk and other technology executives argued that the visas help U.S. companies recruit skilled foreign workers, while some immigration hard-liners in Trump’s political coalition wanted the program ended or sharply restricted. Musk vowed to defend the program after critics attacked its use in technology companies. President-elect Donald Trump then publicly backed H-1B visas, saying he had long supported the program and that it brought skilled workers into the country. The disagreement exposed a conflict between business interests seeking specialized labor and restrictionist supporters who favor tighter limits on immigration. It did not amount to a formal policy decision: Trump had not yet taken office, and his comments did not specify how visa rules would change. The supplied Reuters report describes the public split and Trump’s position; claims that he made concessions to wealthy donors go beyond what it documents.

corrected_wording.label: Claim correction
corrected_wording.text: Remove the claim that Trump offered concessions to wealthy tech donors; the reporting documents his stated support for H-1B visas, not a donor-driven motive.

source_access_notes: Search retrieved the supplied Reuters report on the dispute and Trump’s public support for the program.
rationale: Preserves the coalition conflict while attributing positions to participants and removing the unsupported donor-concession interpretation.

title: Trump Pardons Most January 6 Defendants and Commutes 14 Sentences
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued pardons for most people convicted of offenses related to the January 6 Capitol attack and commuted the sentences of 14 others to time served. His proclamation directed the immediate release of people still imprisoned on related convictions. The clemency included leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys who had been convicted of seditious conspiracy.
description_long: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued sweeping clemency for people convicted in connection with the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. His proclamation commuted the sentences of 14 named individuals to time served and granted pardons to other people convicted of January 6-related offenses. It also directed the attorney general to issue pardon certificates and release those still in prison on covered convictions. The beneficiaries included leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys who had been convicted of seditious conspiracy. Because some sentences were commuted rather than pardoned, describing the action as a pardon for every defendant is imprecise. The clemency affected criminal penalties; it did not overturn the underlying jury verdicts or declare the defendants innocent. The White House described the action as reconciliation, while critics argued it weakened accountability for political violence. The linked 2021 New York Times article covers Trump’s January 6 speech, not the 2025 proclamation.

corrected_wording.label: Scope correction
corrected_wording.text: Use “most January 6 defendants” and specify that 14 sentences were commuted. The proclamation distinguishes commutations from pardons.

source_access_notes: Used the January 20, 2025 White House proclamation and contemporaneous Washington Post report; supplied NYT article is unrelated.
rationale: Corrects the scope by distinguishing commutations from pardons and explains what clemency did and did not change.
